claims.text: At stage-3 refund work is described by three files: docs/team/refund-requirements.md, docs/design/refund-design.md (version 2, rewritten after Payments became a service) and ADR 0003.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3 docs/design/refund-design.md lines 3-6; docs/adr/0003 lines 8-9

claims.text: System design decides the parts of a whole system, how they connect, where each kind of data lives, and how it behaves under load and when a part fails.
A workable order of steps: clarify the requirements, estimate the sizes, sketch the main parts, work out the riskiest parts in detail, look for what limits or stops the whole.

Each step hands the next what it needs: the drivers that matter most say what to estimate, and the sizes say which parts the sketch needs at all (a few requests a day and thousands a second need different parts).
The steps form a loop: a detail that breaks a driver sends the work back to the sketch, a missing answer back to the requirements, and a part that cannot carry the load back to the sketch.

ADR 0003's context names the refund drivers: YC-7, YC-9, YC-10 from refund-requirements.md, plus keeping the gateway's API key in as few places as possible; refund-requirements.md itself does not state that last concern.
Choosing between a broker and plain HTTP calls is a question of how parts connect, so it belongs to step 3 or 4, after the drivers and sizes that decide it.

refund-requirements.md lines 43-50: YC-7 answer within 2 s even if the gateway fails; YC-8 requester and time stored, never changed or deleted; YC-9 never refunded twice; YC-10 automatic resending for at least 24 h before staff take over.

None of refund-requirements.md, refund-design.md and ADR 0003 at stage-3 states how many refunds to expect, and none draws the refund flow as a diagram; the design describes it as numbered prose steps.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3: the three files in full

claims.text: refund-design.md 67-74: v1 kept refund row, order status and email in one transaction; after the split that needs 2PC across two databases, RabbitMQ and the gateway, which cannot work, and a stop halfway would leave rows locked; each step became a local transaction joined by outbox and inbox.

The files hold steps 1, 3 and 4: refund-requirements.md is step 1 (with an open-questions table naming who answers); refund-design.md holds the sketch (numbered list) and the detail (two rejected options); ADR 0003 records splitting Payments out, a step-3 decision costly to undo.
claims.source_hint: refund-requirements.md @ stage-3 lines 52-59; refund-design.md lines 26-80; ADR 0003 lines 30-36

claims.text: Trade-offs: starting from products often finds broken drivers late and records products without reasons; a single line of steps has no planned way back, so it tends to ignore or restart; a loop costs more passes and edits but keeps versions, drivers and rejected options.
The loop pays back when a mistake found late is expensive; a small change that is easy to undo needs one quick pass and no ADR.
Staff list failed refunds at GET /api/v1/refunds?status=failed at stage-3.

refund-design.md's risks say that if the gateway does not accept the idempotency key, item 4 of its numbered refund flow (the job that calls the gateway) must ask for the refund status before each resend (R2).
In a one-hour interview the same five steps apply in minutes each: ask step-1 questions aloud, state assumptions when nobody can answer, keep time for steps 4 and 5.
The database donhang_payments appears only in version 2 of the refund design, after the gateway's API key and money rows made a separate service the chosen option.

Products are answers to drivers and sizes; experience makes steps faster but does not remove them or the way back; an interview squeezes the steps into one sitting while a project spreads them over sprints and files.
refund-design.md opens by stating it is version 2: version 1 (Sprint 15) kept everything in DonHang.Api; version 2 split Payments into DonHang.Payments and rewrote the steps.
